Gastroenterology · published research

Dysphagia

One triple-blind trial found less dysphagia alongside reduced oral mucositis during chemoradiotherapy. Case reports also describe improved swallowing, but the evidence is sparse for causes unrelated to cancer-treatment mucositis.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One triple-blind trial found less dysphagia alongside reduced oral mucositis during chemoradiotherapy. Case reports also describe improved swallowing, but the evidence is sparse for causes unrelated to cancer-treatment mucositis.

Summary of the Evidence

Four human publications are relevant. The exact “Dysphagia” category contains two case reports: one used conventional PBM after breast-cancer hormonal therapy, while the other used water-filtered infrared-A, a heat-based modality rather than conventional PBM. A related three-case cancer-complication series included one patient with dysphagia, and a 221-person randomized trial of oral mucositis measured dysphagia as a secondary outcome. There are no indication-specific animal or laboratory studies.

Human and clinical evidence

The triple-blind randomized trial in 221 head-and-neck cancer patients receiving chemoradiotherapy found lower dysphagia scores in the laser group alongside less severe oral mucositis, pain, and opioid use. Because the study focused on preventing and treating mucositis, it supports a benefit for dysphagia in that specific treatment context, but it does not establish PBM as a general therapy for swallowing disorders (Gautam et al. 2012).

A case report described improved swallowing function after five daily PBM sessions in a breast-cancer patient with chronic dysphagia following hormonal therapy. A separate cancer-related case series also reported improvement in its dysphagia case, but did not provide a controlled comparison. These observations fit the direction of the randomized mucositis trial, while offering little certainty for other causes of dysphagia (El Mobadder et al. 2019; El Mobadder et al. 2019).

The other exact-category case used water-filtered infrared-A on the neck and chest together with acetylcysteine. Salivation and mucus decreased and oral intake improved over time, but the treatment was thermal infrared and the co-treatment prevents attribution to light alone (Hoffmann et al. 2017).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for dysphagia was identified in these records.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell-culture or ex-vivo evidence for dysphagia was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The randomized mucositis trial used 632.8-nm red visible He-Ne laser, 3 J per point and 36–40 J per session, five days per week during a 6.5-week chemoradiotherapy course. The single PBM case used 980-nm near-infrared light at 3 J per point over five days. The wIRA case used prolonged infrared-A heating rather than a standard PBM protocol. These approaches target different causes and tissues, and have not been compared directly.

Interpretation

The randomized result shows less dysphagia in patients receiving PBM for chemoradiotherapy-induced oral mucositis, which is a clinically relevant supportive-care outcome. The case reports point in a similar direction but cannot establish cause. Evidence is strongest for this cancer-treatment context and remains very limited for neurologic, structural, or other forms of dysphagia.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for dysphagia associated with chemoradiotherapy-induced oral mucositis Very low for other causes of dysphagia
Publications and records4 relevant articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A triple-blind randomized trial of 221 people found lower dysphagia scores when red laser was used to prevent and treat oral mucositis during chemoradiotherapy. A separate PBM case report and a small case series also described improved swallowing, while the other exact-category case used heat-producing water-filtered infrared. A swallowing-focused trial would clarify effects beyond mucositis.
